metadata.title: The Performance Gap
metadata.description: Address a team member's declining performance while balancing empathy, accountability, and team dynamics
learningObjectives: Learn to address team dynamics around performance
metadata.author: Conflict Management Training Team

player.name: You
player.description: A team lead balancing friendship, leadership responsibilities, and team performance

chris.name: Chris
chris.description: Previously reliable team member now struggling with performance and personal issues

team_members.name: Team
team_members.description: Frustrated team members who are picking up extra work due to Chris's performance issues

manager.name: Leslie
manager.description: Your manager who expects the team to deliver but values employee support

settings.location: Software development office with individual workstations

content.title: The Team's Growing Frustration
content.text: Your team is falling behind on the sprint goals, and you notice a pattern: Chris has missed three deadlines in six weeks, submitted code with unusual bugs, and seems disengaged in meetings. Yesterday, two team members privately expressed frustration about picking up Chris's unfinished work. Chris used to be one of your strongest contributors. You need to address this situation before it affects the entire team's morale and delivery.
content.speaker: narrator

choices.text: Have a private, supportive conversation with Chris to understand what's happening
Schedule a formal performance discussion focused on work standards and expectations
Address the workload distribution issue with the whole team present
Consult with your manager Leslie about how to handle the performance issues

content.title: Opening the Door to Understanding
content.text: You invite Chris for coffee away from the office. 'I've noticed you seem stressed lately, and I wanted to check in - both as your team lead and as someone who cares about you.' Chris hesitates, then opens up: 'There's a family situation that's been taking a lot out of me, and some personal things on top of it. I'm barely keeping my head above water, but I didn't want to burden the team with personal stuff.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Creating a safe, private space for conversation allows the real issues to surface. Understanding the context doesn't excuse performance problems but helps identify appropriate support and solutions.
feedback.consequences: Chris feels supported and trusted; real issues are identified

choices.text: Offer support resources and work together on a performance improvement plan
Suggest temporary workload reduction while Chris addresses personal issues
Express empathy but emphasize that work standards must be maintained
Suggest Chris share appropriate details with the team to reduce frustration

content.title: Building a Bridge Forward
content.text: You and Chris work together on a plan: temporarily reduce Chris's workload by 20%, connect Chris with the Employee Assistance Program for confidential support, establish weekly check-ins to monitor progress and provide guidance, and set clear milestones for returning to full performance within 8 weeks. Chris is grateful: 'I was afraid you'd think I was making excuses. Having a plan makes this feel manageable.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: This approach balances empathy with accountability by creating structure and support while maintaining performance expectations. It addresses root causes rather than just symptoms.
feedback.consequences: Chris has clear path forward with support; team gets transparency and timeline

choices.text: Help Chris communicate the plan to the team in an appropriate way
Focus on intensive monitoring and support during the transition period
Document the plan formally to protect both Chris and the team

content.title: Team Understanding and Support
content.text: Chris shares with the team: 'I'm dealing with some significant personal challenges that have affected my work. I'm working with our team lead on a support plan, and I'll be taking on a slightly reduced workload for the next few weeks while I get back on track.' The team responds with understanding and offers help. One colleague says: 'We've all been there - let us know how we can support you.' The team's frustration turns into collective support.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Transparent communication transforms team frustration into support by helping colleagues understand the situation. This builds team resilience and psychological safety.
feedback.consequences: Team cohesion strengthens, Chris feels supported, performance pressure reduces while accountability remains

endings.title: Team Resilience Built
endings.description: The team develops a culture of supporting members through difficult times while maintaining performance standards, becoming stronger and more resilient.
endings.reflection: How can transparency about struggles create stronger teams rather than weakness?

content.title: Focusing on Standards
content.text: You schedule a formal meeting with Chris. 'I need to discuss your recent performance. You've missed three deadlines, and the code quality has been inconsistent. What's your plan to get back on track?' Chris becomes defensive: 'I'm doing my best. These deadlines are unrealistic anyway.' The conversation becomes tense, with Chris shutting down rather than opening up about the real issues.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: While performance standards are important, leading with criticism without understanding context often puts people on the defensive and misses opportunities to address root causes.
feedback.consequences: Chris becomes defensive, real issues remain hidden, relationship trust decreases

choices.text: Recognize the approach isn't working and shift to a more supportive tone
Make clear that continued performance issues will result in formal disciplinary action
Ask Chris to share their perspective on what's making the work challenging

content.title: Recovering from a Rough Start
content.text: You pause and change your approach: 'I can see this conversation started off on the wrong foot. I'm concerned about you and the team, and I want to understand what's really going on so we can figure out how to help.' Chris relaxes slightly: 'I appreciate that. I guess I felt attacked and got defensive. There are some things happening in my personal life that are making work really hard right now.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Course-correcting when an approach isn't working shows emotional intelligence and can rescue difficult conversations, though it requires rebuilding trust that was initially damaged.
feedback.consequences: Trust partially restored, Chris begins to open up, but initial defensiveness lingers

choices.text: Focus on rebuilding trust and understanding Chris's situation
Acknowledge personal challenges while maintaining performance expectations

content.title: Seeking Guidance
content.text: You discuss the situation with Leslie: 'Chris has been struggling lately, and it's affecting the team. I want to handle this supportively but also need to maintain our delivery commitments.' Leslie responds: 'I appreciate you bringing this to me. What's your read on whether this is a capability issue or something else? We have resources available to help, but we also need to be fair to the rest of the team.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Seeking guidance shows good judgment, but it's important to balance getting support with maintaining your team leadership role and direct relationship with team members.
feedback.consequences: You gain management support and resources, but need to maintain direct leadership relationship

choices.text: Work with Leslie to develop a supportive approach that addresses both performance and personal issues
Suggest involving HR to ensure proper documentation and support resources
Take Leslie's guidance but handle the conversation directly with Chris yourself

content.title: Leadership Alignment
content.text: You and Leslie develop a comprehensive approach: you'll have the initial supportive conversation with Chris, Leslie will provide backup resources including EAP and flexible work arrangements, and you'll both monitor progress with regular check-ins. This ensures Chris gets proper support while maintaining team accountability. The approach successfully addresses both Chris's personal challenges and team performance needs.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Collaborating with management creates comprehensive support while maintaining your direct leadership relationship. This approach provides resources and backup while keeping you as the primary relationship owner.
feedback.consequences: Chris receives comprehensive support, team sees effective leadership, management confidence in your abilities increases

endings.title: Supported Leadership
endings.description: The collaborative approach with management becomes a model for handling similar situations, creating a supportive yet accountable team culture.
endings.reflection: How can collaboration with management enhance rather than undermine direct leadership relationships?

content.title: Awkward Public Exposure
content.text: In the team meeting, you address workload distribution: 'I've noticed some tasks are taking longer than expected, and I want to make sure we're supporting each other.' Chris looks uncomfortable as team members mention specific delayed deliverables. The conversation becomes awkward, with Chris feeling singled out and team members unsure whether they can speak honestly about the impact on their work.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Addressing individual performance issues in group settings often creates embarrassment and doesn't allow for the private, supportive conversation needed to understand and address root causes.
feedback.consequences: Chris feels publicly shamed, team becomes uncomfortable with direct feedback, real issues remain unaddressed

choices.text: Quickly pivot to general topics and plan to follow up with Chris privately
Continue the public discussion to ensure transparency and accountability
Shift focus to how the team can better support each other during challenging periods

content.title: Repairing the Mistake
content.text: You quickly shift the meeting to general project topics and catch Chris afterward: 'I realize that meeting was awkward - I should have talked with you privately first. Can we have coffee tomorrow to discuss how I can better support you?' Chris appreciates the acknowledgment: 'Thanks for recognizing that. I was feeling pretty exposed in there. I'd appreciate a private conversation.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Recognizing and correcting a mistake shows emotional intelligence and can prevent further damage to the relationship, though some trust repair is needed.
feedback.consequences: Trust partially restored, Chris appreciates the correction, but some embarrassment from public exposure remains

choices.text: Focus the private conversation on rebuilding trust and understanding Chris's needs
Also address the team dynamic to ensure Chris doesn't feel isolated

content.title: Breathing Room Approach
content.text: You arrange for Chris to take on 75% of normal workload for the next month: 'Let's reduce your sprint commitment while you handle these personal challenges. The team can absorb the extra work temporarily.' Chris is relieved but concerned: 'I appreciate this, but I don't want the team to resent me for not pulling my weight. And I'm worried about falling behind professionally.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Temporary support can be helpful, but without clear communication to the team and plans for return to full performance, it may create resentment and doesn't address skill development needs.
feedback.consequences: Chris gets immediate relief but worries about team dynamics and professional development

choices.text: Work with Chris to communicate the temporary plan transparently to the team
Use the reduced workload time for skill development and process improvement
Keep the arrangement private and handle team questions as they arise

content.title: Collective Understanding
content.text: Chris shares with the team: 'I'm going through some personal challenges and will be working at reduced capacity for a few weeks with a clear plan to get back to full strength.' The team responds supportively, with offers to help and understanding about the temporary arrangement. One teammate says: 'We've all needed support at different times - we've got your back.' The temporary arrangement works because everyone understands it's temporary and purposeful.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Transparent communication about temporary support creates team understanding and prevents resentment. It models a supportive team culture while maintaining clear expectations.
feedback.consequences: Team supports Chris through difficult period, culture of mutual support develops, performance expectations remain clear

endings.title: Mutual Support Culture
endings.description: The team develops a culture where members support each other through difficult times, creating resilience and loyalty while maintaining performance standards.
endings.reflection: How can temporary accommodations strengthen rather than weaken team performance culture?

content.title: The Ultimatum Backfires
content.text: You escalate: 'If performance doesn't improve immediately, we'll need to consider formal disciplinary action.' Chris responds angrily: 'Fine, I'll start looking for another job where people understand that life happens.' The relationship deteriorates rapidly. Chris does minimum work while job searching, team morale drops as they watch the conflict unfold, and you lose a formerly valuable team member who could have been supported through a difficult period.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Threats without understanding root causes often escalate conflicts and can result in losing valuable employees who could have been supported through temporary difficulties.
feedback.consequences: Chris becomes disengaged and seeks other employment, team witnesses poor conflict resolution, valuable employee and knowledge lost

endings.title: Lost Talent and Trust
endings.description: The harsh approach results in losing a previously strong performer and damages team trust in leadership's support during difficult times.
endings.reflection: What are the long-term costs of prioritizing immediate performance pressure over understanding and supporting team members?

content.title: Growth Through Challenge
content.text: You and Chris use the reduced workload time for professional development: learning new technologies, improving code review processes, and mentoring junior developers. This approach helps Chris feel professionally valued while managing personal stress. When Chris returns to full capacity, the new skills benefit the entire team. The challenge becomes a growth opportunity rather than just a problem to manage.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Using support time for development creates positive outcomes for both individual and team. It maintains professional engagement while accommodating personal challenges.
feedback.consequences: Chris grows professionally while managing personal challenges, team benefits from new skills and processes, positive precedent set

endings.title: Challenge as Catalyst
endings.description: The approach of using support periods for development becomes a team standard, turning temporary performance challenges into growth opportunities.
endings.reflection: How can performance support periods become opportunities for professional development rather than just accommodation?

content.title: Process Over Relationship
content.text: You involve HR, who initiates formal performance documentation and improvement processes. While this protects the organization legally, it creates a formal, transactional relationship with Chris. The process works to address performance standards, but the personal trust and team relationship are damaged. Chris improves performance to meet requirements but loses the engagement and innovation that made them valuable previously.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Formal processes ensure compliance and documentation but can damage relationships and reduce employee engagement. They should be balanced with supportive leadership approaches.
feedback.consequences: Performance standards maintained but at cost of engagement, creativity, and team relationship trust

endings.title: Compliance Over Culture
endings.description: The formal approach solves the immediate performance issue but creates a more transactional, less innovative team culture.
endings.reflection: What are the trade-offs between formal performance processes and relationship-based leadership approaches?

content.title: Kind but Firm
content.text: You tell Chris you're sorry they're dealing with so much, and that you appreciate their honesty. Then you add: 'At the same time, the team is depending on these deliverables, and I need the standards to hold.' Chris nods slowly. 'Right. So I just need to try harder.' The conversation is still warm, but Chris seems to be carrying the same weight as before.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Acknowledging Chris's situation while keeping expectations clear is better than choosing only one, and it is honest about what the team needs. But without concrete support, it asks Chris to meet the same bar on their own. A middle position can leave both needs only half met.
feedback.consequences: Chris feels heard but not helped; expectations are clear, but the path to meeting them isn't

choices.text: Ask what support would make the standard reachable, and build a plan together
Agree on a smaller set of firm commitments for the next two sprints

content.title: Whose Story to Tell
content.text: You suggest that telling the team something might ease the tension. Chris tenses: 'I don't want everyone knowing my business.' You clarify that it's entirely Chris's choice, and that even 'I'm dealing with something personal' would be enough. Chris relaxes a little: 'Maybe. But I'd want to have a plan first, so it doesn't sound like I'm just asking for a pass.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Transparency can turn team frustration into support, but this is Chris's information to share. Suggesting it too early can feel like a condition of getting help. Listening to Chris's hesitation, and making clear the choice is theirs, keeps trust intact.
feedback.consequences: Chris is open to sharing something, on their own terms and once there is a plan

choices.text: Build a support plan together first, so Chris has something concrete to share
Respect Chris's privacy and tell the team only that workloads are being adjusted

content.title: A Close Eye
content.text: You add daily check-ins, review each of Chris's pull requests yourself, and quietly pick up two of Chris's tickets. Chris's output steadies. After two weeks, though, Chris says: 'I know you mean well, but the daily check-ins make me feel like I'm being watched.' Meanwhile your own work has slipped, and the team still doesn't know why their lead is so busy.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Intensive support can help someone through a hard stretch, and Chris's work did improve. But heavy monitoring can read as distrust, and absorbing the extra work yourself is hard to sustain. Support works best when the person helps decide what kind they need.
feedback.consequences: Chris's work stabilizes, but Chris feels watched and your own workload suffers

endings.title: Support That Smothers
endings.description: Chris gets back on track, but you learn that more oversight isn't always more support.
endings.reflection: How can you tell the difference between support someone finds helpful and support that feels like surveillance?

content.title: Putting It in Writing
content.text: You write up the support plan with its milestones, share it with Leslie, and ask Chris to review and sign it. Chris reads it twice. 'Is this a performance improvement plan?' You explain that it records the support as well as the expectations. Chris signs and meets the milestones over the next two months, but the warmth of your coffee conversation doesn't quite come back.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Documentation creates clarity and protects both Chris and the team if things go wrong later. But adding formality right after a vulnerable conversation can feel like a warning. Putting the organization's protection first is a legitimate choice, and it costs some closeness.
feedback.consequences: Expectations are clear and Chris improves, but the relationship becomes more guarded

endings.title: Clear but Cooler
endings.description: The written plan works, though Chris is more careful about what they share with you afterward.
endings.reflection: When does putting an agreement in writing build trust, and when does it signal a lack of trust?

content.title: A Question, Late
content.text: You pause and ask: 'What's making the work hard right now, from your side?' Chris is still guarded, but answers: 'Honestly? There's a lot going on outside work. And the last few sprints, the estimates haven't matched the actual work.' It is only part of the picture, but it's more than you had five minutes ago.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Asking for Chris's perspective is the right move, even midway through a conversation that started badly. Because it opened with criticism, Chris shares only part of the story. Listening late still helps; it just takes more effort to rebuild the trust that the opening cost.
feedback.consequences: Chris shares two real issues - personal strain and a sprint-sizing problem - but remains guarded

choices.text: Acknowledge you started too hard, and ask what would help with both issues
Take the estimate point seriously and agree on fewer, firm commitments while you review sprint sizing
Steer back to the deadlines and make clear what happens if they keep slipping

content.title: Slowing Down
content.text: You put your notes aside. 'I came in too hard, and I'm sorry. I'd like to understand what's going on before we talk about deadlines.' Chris takes a breath and explains that a family situation has been taking a lot of their time and energy, and that they've been trying to keep it from affecting work. Together you talk through which parts of the job have been hardest to keep up with.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Owning your part in a rough start makes it safe for the other person to be honest. Repairing trust takes more time than starting well would have, but it now makes a real plan possible.
feedback.consequences: Chris opens up and is ready to work on a plan with you

choices.text: Build a support plan together with clear milestones
Offer a temporarily lighter workload while things settle

content.title: Adjusted, Not Lowered
content.text: You and Chris agree on a middle path: for the next two sprints, Chris commits to fewer tickets, each with a firm date, and you'll check in briefly once a week. 'The bar is the same,' you explain. 'We're just narrowing what you're responsible for while things are hard.' Chris agrees, though they ask: 'What do we tell the team about why I have less on my plate?'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Reducing scope while keeping quality and deadlines firm gives Chris breathing room without dropping accountability. Both sides give a little. The open question is the team: an adjustment no one explains can look like favoritism.
feedback.consequences: Chris has a realistic workload and clear commitments; the team still needs to be considered

choices.text: Ask Chris how they would like the team told about the adjusted workload
Keep the adjustment between you and Chris

content.title: Leslie's Advice, Your Conversation
content.text: Leslie suggests you open with care, describe specific impacts rather than judgments, and mention the Employee Assistance Program. You meet Chris privately and follow that approach. Chris is surprised but responds: 'I didn't realize it was that noticeable. There's a family situation that's been taking a lot out of me.' Chris seems relieved the conversation is with you and not with Leslie.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Following your manager's guidance while keeping the conversation in your own hands gives you experienced advice without passing the relationship upward. The trade-off is that you're using someone else's approach, which can feel less natural, and it's worth adapting it to what you know about Chris.
feedback.consequences: Chris opens up to you directly, with Leslie's resources available in the background

choices.text: Work out a support plan with Chris, using the resources Leslie mentioned
Offer Chris a temporarily reduced workload
Express empathy but make clear that the deadlines still need to be met

content.title: Accountability in Public
content.text: You keep the discussion going, and teammates list the tasks that slipped. Chris answers in short sentences, then stops talking altogether. After the meeting, Chris stays heads-down and stops speaking up in standups. Over the next weeks, other team members become less willing to mention when they're falling behind, since they've seen how it gets handled.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Pressing for accountability in front of the group puts the team's frustration ahead of Chris's dignity. Public pressure rarely reveals why someone is struggling, and it teaches everyone watching to hide problems instead of raising them early.
feedback.consequences: Chris withdraws, the team learns to hide struggles, and the real causes stay hidden

endings.title: Silence Spreads
endings.description: The public approach doesn't fix Chris's performance and makes the whole team less likely to raise problems early.
endings.reflection: What does a team learn from watching how one person's struggles are handled in public?

content.title: From Blame to Team Habits
content.text: You change direction: 'Everyone hits a rough patch sometimes. How can we flag when we're overloaded, before work starts slipping?' The team suggests raising capacity concerns at standup, pairing on risky tickets, and a quick workload check before each sprint. Chris stays quiet but looks less tense. The meeting ends calmer, though nothing has been said to Chris directly.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Turning the conversation toward shared habits lowers the heat and builds norms that help everyone. But it is a general fix for a specific situation: Chris still needs a private conversation, and the teammates who raised concerns may feel their point was sidestepped.
feedback.consequences: The team has better habits for flagging overload, but Chris's situation hasn't been addressed

choices.text: Follow up with Chris privately after the meeting
Let the new team habits do the work and avoid singling Chris out

content.title: Good Habits, Missing Conversation
content.text: The team uses its new habits, and capacity check-ins become routine. Chris never brings up their own workload, though, and you never ask. Deadlines keep slipping, more slowly than before. A month later, a teammate asks you directly why nothing has changed with Chris.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Team norms are valuable, and avoiding a hard conversation can feel like protecting someone. But habits can't replace a direct conversation when one person is clearly struggling. Avoiding it leaves Chris without support and leaves the team doubting that problems get handled.
feedback.consequences: Team habits improve, but Chris's situation goes unaddressed and the team's trust in your leadership drops

endings.title: Systems Without Support
endings.description: The team's processes improve, but the person who most needed a conversation never got one.
endings.reflection: When is a team-wide fix a way of avoiding a conversation with one person?

content.title: Starting Over, Privately
content.text: Over coffee, you start by owning the meeting: 'I put you on the spot in front of everyone, and that wasn't fair.' Chris accepts the apology and, after a while, explains that things at home have been very demanding and they haven't known how to bring it up. Chris asks that the team not be told the details.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Repairing trust before talking about performance makes an honest conversation possible. It takes time, and you are starting from behind after the meeting, but Chris is now willing to work on the problem with you.
feedback.consequences: Chris trusts you enough to talk, and has asked for privacy about the details

choices.text: Build a support plan together with clear milestones
Agree on a smaller set of firm commitments for the next two sprints

content.title: Easing the Team's Frustration
content.text: You talk with the two teammates who raised concerns. You acknowledge the extra work they've been carrying and ask them to hold off on judging Chris, without sharing anything private. They appreciate being heard, but one asks: 'Okay, but what's the plan? We can't keep absorbing this indefinitely.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Smoothing the team's feelings helps keep Chris from being isolated, and recognizing the extra load matters. But without a plan, you are asking teammates to keep absorbing work on trust. Accommodation buys time; it doesn't solve the problem.
feedback.consequences: The team feels heard but wants to see a concrete plan

choices.text: Talk with Chris privately, then come back to the team with a concrete plan
Quietly lighten Chris's load and handle team questions as they come up

content.title: The Quiet Arrangement
content.text: You keep Chris's adjusted workload between the two of you. For a few weeks it works: Chris's output steadies and their privacy is protected. But the team notices Chris getting fewer tickets with no explanation. Talk of favoritism starts, and one teammate raises it with Leslie. Chris feels protected but increasingly isolated from the team.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Protecting someone's privacy is a real value, and Chris did get relief. But avoiding any explanation leaves the team to invent its own, which often turns into resentment. Chris's details can stay private while the arrangement itself is still acknowledged.
feedback.consequences: Chris gets relief, but the team grows resentful and Chris becomes isolated

endings.title: Protected but Isolated
endings.description: The private arrangement helps Chris in the short term, but the unexplained change damages trust on the team.
endings.reflection: How can you protect someone's privacy without keeping the team in the dark about decisions that affect them?

keyTakeaways: Performance issues often have underlying causes that need to be understood
Balancing empathy with accountability requires collaborative problem-solving
Private, supportive conversations are usually more effective than formal criticism
Team transparency about challenges can build support rather than resentment
Early intervention and support often prevent the need for disciplinary action
furtherReading: The Culture Code by Daniel Coyle
First, Break All the Rules by Marcus Buckingham
practiceQuestions: How do you balance empathy with accountability in performance situations?
What signs might indicate that performance issues have personal rather than professional causes?
When is transparency helpful versus harmful in team performance situations?
